lines: Deliberate
Firepower
Van Fleet's army in Korea in 1951 relied on registered fire and
forward ammunition stocks. Deliberate infantry assaults gain fire
superiority, but assembling fire plans slows preparation and
increases supply demand.
Mobile Raiding
Warfare
South African mobile battle groups used rapid concentration and
flanking attacks in the 1970s and 1980s. Forward loads support short
advances; delayed resupply beyond this reserve brings greater supply
penalties and weak fixed defence.
Cohesive Unit
Rotation
British unit rotation and the later American COHORT programme
kept crews and companies together through training and service.
Stable teams preserve experience and cohesion, but require longer
training and a costlier personnel system.
Integrated Support
Commands
Logistical commands in Korea and corps support commands in the
1960s united supply, workshops, recovery and medical services.
Integrated support sustains the fighting force, but needs more
personnel and slows the march column.
Forest
Envelopment
Finnish motti operations isolated road-bound columns through
forest movement, also in summer campaigns in 1941 to 1944. Foot
infantry and dismounted specialists gain local mobility and surprise,
with less central battle preparation.
Heliborne Reaction
Forces
Rhodesian Fireforce from 1974 linked helicopter-borne blocking
groups with reconnaissance and follow-up forces. Light assault
groups need considerable fuel and fare poorly in frontal attacks on
prepared fortifications.
Assault Breaching
British specialist formations in 1943 and 1944 and Egyptian engineers
at Suez in 1973 demonstrated deliberate obstacle assaults. Infantry
rehearses crossings and attacks on fortified positions, increasing
training and supply requirements.
Key Zone Defence
Austria's Raumverteidigung prepared key routes for defence. Forts
and river positions support local resistance, but moving these
defenders disrupts their organisation. An alternative to Territorial
Defence Forces.
Coastal Denial
Swedish coastal-defence planning in the 1950s combined protected
batteries, local observation and mobile reserves. Troops contest a
landing before a bridgehead forms, trading offensive breakthrough
for specialised coastal upkeep.
Opposing Force
Exercises
An active opposing force and structured reviews expose weaknesses
in field training. The National Training Center, operational in 1981,
became a later instrumented model. Such proficiency needs more
training time and personnel.
Mission Rehearsal
Egyptian preparations for the Suez crossing in 1973 demonstrated
the value of repeated mission practice. Specialist formations
rehearse routes, timings and assaults, gaining proficiency through
longer and more expensive training.
Institutional
Combat Learning
Korean and Vietnam War lessons systems preceded the permanent
Center for Army Lessons Learned established in 1985. Reports and
instructor exchanges spread operational experience, requiring
evaluation staff and additional training.
Guided Anti Armour
Integration
Egyptian defence in 1973 combined infantry with prepared anti-tank
positions. Guided weapons improve anti-armour fire, but specialist
companies need costly upkeep and sacrifice soft-target fire and
offensive breakthrough.
Counterfire
Coordination
Observers and early radars supported artillery in Vietnam; more
capable networks followed later. Coordinated fire improves the
guns, but needs more supply and exposes information through radar
and radio emissions.
